title: First In, Last Out: The Portuguese in India
sources: Rajiv Ahir, A Brief History of Modern India, ch. 3 "Advent of the Europeans in India" (Portuguese section): core narrative, Albuquerque sati ban, persecution in Goa, Hooghly slave trade and Mumtaz Mahal episode, the Portuguese governor's sword-and-cross remark (paraphrased)
Corrections to Ahir applied: 1508 defeat at Chaul (not "off Diu" 1507); pilot unnamed ("a Gujarati pilot"); Nuno da Cunha; Bahadur Shah died 13 Feb 1537 after talks aboard a Portuguese ship
Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape early 1488 (Wikipedia "Bartolomeu Dias"; SAHO; History.com)
Vasco da Gama reached Calicut 20 May 1498 (Wikipedia "Portuguese India"; herodote.net)
Fort Manuel, Cochin, 1503: first European fort in India (Wikipedia "Fort Emmanuel"; WorldHistory.org "Portuguese Cochin")
Battle of Chaul March 1508, Lourenco de Almeida killed; Battle of Diu 3 Feb 1509 (Wikipedia "Battle of Chaul"; Britannica "Lourenco de Almeida")
Goa taken March 1510, lost May 1510, retaken 25 Nov 1510 (Britannica "History of Goa"; Wikipedia "Portuguese conquest of Goa")
Capital moved from Cochin to Goa 1530 (Wikipedia "Portuguese India")
Bahadur Shah died 13 Feb 1537 off Diu during talks aboard a Portuguese ship; accounts differ on how (Wikipedia "Bahadur Shah of Gujarat", "Siege of Diu (1538)")
Jesuit mission (Acquaviva, Monserrate, Henriques) reached Fatehpur Sikri Feb/March 1580 (Dawn; Wikipedia "Antoni de Montserrat")
William Hawkins at Surat, August 1608 (GKToday); Battle of Swally, Nov 1612 (Wikipedia "Battle of Swally")
Siege of Hooghly, June-Sept 1632, about three months (Wikipedia "Siege of Hooghly"; Royal Collection "The Capture of Port Hugli")
Dutch take Cochin (Jan 1663) and Cannanore (Feb 1663) (Wikipedia "Dutch conquest of Malabar")
Marathas take Bassein 1739 (not independently re-checked this session)
Operation Vijay, 18-19 Dec 1961: Goa, Daman and Diu annexed by India (Wikipedia "Annexation of Goa"; USI of India)

lines.text: In fourteen ninety-eight,
lines.shot: dawn sea, 4 parallax layers, sun lifts → "ninety-eight"

lines.text: three small ships dropped anchor off the coast of Kerala.
lines.shot: 3 caravels slide in from right, anchors drop → "anchor"

lines.text: Their crews had sailed for almost eleven months,
lines.shot: deck close-up: hourglass, calendar leaves peel off → "months"

lines.text: all the way around Africa,
lines.shot: real map, crimson route Lisbon→Cape→Calicut draws on → "Africa"

lines.text: for one thing: pepper.
lines.shot: pepper vine close-up, a peppercorn rolls into a sack → "pepper"

lines.text: They had just started a story
lines.shot: quill writes a first line, page lifts

lines.text: that would last four hundred and sixty-three years.
lines.shot: gold ribbon 1498 → 1961, slip FIRST IN, LAST OUT → "years"

lines.text: Chapter one. The Spice Problem.
In fourteen fifty-three,
lines.shot: map Europe–Med, era bar tick 1453 turns crimson

lines.text: the Ottoman Turks captured Constantinople,
and the old roads to the East fell into other hands.
Indian pepper, silk and cotton still reached Europe,
lines.shot: three goods pop on the route one by one

lines.text: but only through Arab middlemen,
lines.shot: sack passes hand to hand along 4 merchants

lines.text: and every one of them took a cut.
lines.shot: a coin drops at each hand, price slip grows

lines.text: So little Portugal, on the edge of the Atlantic,
lines.shot: map pulls back: tiny Portugal at the Atlantic edge

lines.text: made a bold bet:
if you can't go through, go around.
lines.shot: arrow hits padlock, bends around Africa → "around"

lines.text: Prince Henry, the Navigator,
lines.shot: Henry (dark hood) points at wall map

lines.text: pushed ship after ship down the coast of Africa,
lines.shot: caravels step down the coast, each leaves a pin

lines.text: and in fourteen eighty-eight, Bartholomew Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope.
lines.caps: in *1488, | Bartholomew *Dias | rounded the *Cape | of Good *Hope.
lines.shot: Dias's ship rounds the Cape, slip CAPE OF GOOD HOPE

lines.text: The door to the Indian Ocean was open.
lines.shot: paper wall, door-shaped gap swings open, sea light → "open"

lines.text: Chapter two. Hello, Kalikut.
Ten years later, Vasco da Gama walked through it.
lines.shot: da Gama steps through the paper door

lines.text: In East Africa, he picked up a Gujarati pilot
lines.shot: Malindi harbour, pilot with kamal boards → "pilot"

lines.text: who knew the monsoon winds,
lines.shot: wind arrows push the sail across the map

lines.text: and in May fourteen ninety-eight, he reached Kalikut.
Kalikut's Hindu king, the Zam-oh-rin,
grew rich by welcoming traders,
lines.shot: many-coloured sails in port, coins into chest

lines.text: so he welcomed this one too.
The Arab merchants were far less happy.
lines.shot: Arab merchant frowns over his ledger

lines.text: For centuries, Indians, Arabs, Africans and Chinese
lines.shot: ocean map fills with small sails of 4 colours

lines.text: had shared this ocean by unwritten rules:
everyone traded, but nobody owned the sea.
The Portuguese wanted to own it.
lines.shot: one blue sail grows, the others shrink back → "own"

lines.text: Da Gama sailed home with a cargo worth a fortune,
lines.shot: laden ship sails west on the route

lines.text: because pepper that cost little in Kerala
lines.shot: spice scale: one sack vs two coins

lines.text: sold for many times as much in Europe.
lines.caps: sold for *many times | as much in *Europe.

lines.text: Chapter three. Traders Become Raiders.
The next fleet, under Pedro Cabral,
set up a trading post in Kalikut in fifteen hundred.
lines.shot: factory hut with blue flag goes up

lines.text: Locals attacked it,
and several Portuguese died.
lines.shot: torn flag, empty stools, dropped cap (no people)

lines.text: Cabral struck back:
he burned Arab ships in the harbour
and turned his cannons on the city.
Then he sailed south, and made friends with Kalikut's rivals,
lines.shot: map: ship slides south along Malabar

lines.text: Cochin and Kanna-nore.
lines.shot: handshake slips pinned on Cochin + Cannanore

lines.text: When da Gama returned,
lines.shot: da Gama's blue sail back on the horizon

lines.text: and demanded that the Zam-oh-rin expel every Arab trader,
lines.shot: da Gama holds out a demand letter

lines.text: the Zam-oh-rin refused,
lines.shot: Zamorin shakes head, tears the paper

lines.text: and the trading posts quietly grew walls and guns.
In fifteen-oh-three, the first Portuguese fort rose at Cochin.
Chapter four. Rule the Water.
In fifteen-oh-five, Portugal sent its first governor,
Francisco de Al-may-da, with a simple plan:
forget the land, control the water.
lines.shot: blue wash floods the sea on the map → "water"

lines.text: Every ship now needed a Portuguese pass,
or risked being seized.
lines.shot: a dhow with no pass: chain across its bow

lines.text: That threatened Gujarat, Egypt,
and even the merchants of Venice,
lines.shot: Venice pin, crimson thread links the three

lines.text: so Egypt and Gujarat joined forces.
In fifteen-oh-eight, at Chowl, they beat the Portuguese,
lines.shot: night: one Portuguese ship silhouette sinks under navy wash

lines.text: and Al-may-da's own son was killed.
lines.shot: empty helmet on a table, candle

lines.text: A year later, off Dee-oo,
Al-may-da destroyed their fleet.
lines.shot: their paper sails fall one by one

lines.text: His lesson was clear:
whoever rules the sea holds India.
lines.shot: slip "Rule the sea, hold India" — paraphrase · Almeida

lines.text: Chapter five. Al-boo-kerk's Goa.
His successor, Afonso de Al-boo-kerk, went further.
lines.shot: Albuquerque (very long white beard, tall hat)

lines.text: He built strongholds at every gate of the ocean,
lines.shot: map: padlock-forts on the sea's doors

lines.text: from Hor-mooz to Muh-lakka,
lines.shot: pins pop at Hormuz, then Malacca

lines.text: and in fifteen-ten, he captured Goa from the Sultan of Bee-jah-poor.
He told his men to marry local women and settle down.
They brought tobacco and cashew,
and Al-boo-kerk banned sati in Goa.
But Muslims, Portugal's old rivals,
were bitterly persecuted.
By fifteen-thirty, Goa was the capital,
and in fifteen thirty-seven, Sultan Bahadur Shah of Gujarat
went aboard a Portuguese ship for talks,
lines.shot: he steps onto a ship at dusk

lines.text: and never came home.
lines.shot: his turban floating on dark water

lines.text: Chapter six. Priests and Emperors.
In fifteen-eighty, two Jesuit priests from Goa
reached the court of Emperor Akbar,
who loved debating religion.
lines.shot: Akbar among scholars of several faiths

lines.text: The Portuguese dreamed that if the emperor converted,
Mughal India would follow.
He didn't.
Back in Goa, after the Inquisition arrived,
Hindus were persecuted too.
Then, in sixteen-oh-eight, an Englishman, William Hawkins,
landed at Surat with a letter from his king.
lines.caps: landed at *Surat | a *letter | from his king.

lines.text: The Portuguese tried everything to stop him,
but in sixteen twelve, English ships beat a Portuguese fleet near Surat,
lines.shot: small English sails vs bigger fleet; big sails tear

lines.text: and Emperor Jahangir, who had no navy, was impressed.
Chapter seven. The Fall.
The worst blow came in Bengal.
At Hoog-lee, Portuguese traders ran a cruel slave trade,
seizing Hindu and Muslim children,
lines.shot: ledger page with a broken chain

lines.text: and, chroniclers say, even took two slave girls of Empress Mum-taz Mahal.
lines.caps: chroniclers say, | two girls of | *Mumtaz Mahal.
lines.shot: Mughal seal over an empty doorway

lines.text: In sixteen thirty-two, Shah Jahan's army besieged Hoog-lee,
lines.shot: seal stamps the map, tents ring the port

lines.text: and three months later, the Portuguese were gone from Bengal.
Everything else was slipping too.
Portugal's crown had passed to Spain,
lines.shot: crown slides onto a Spanish crown

lines.text: dragging it into Spain's wars,
Brazil was now worth more than India,
lines.shot: map swings west, coins roll to Brazil

lines.text: and the sea route was no longer a secret.
lines.caps: the sea route | no longer a *secret.
lines.shot: route map copied onto Dutch + English parchment

lines.text: By sixteen sixty-three, the Dutch had taken every Portuguese fort on the Malabar coast.
lines.shot: Malabar forts flip to Dutch flags one by one

lines.text: In seventeen thirty-nine, the Marathas took Bassein.
One Portuguese governor put it best:
they came with a sword in one hand and a cross in the other,
lines.caps: a *sword in one hand, | a *cross in the other,

lines.text: filled their pockets with gold,
and grew too heavy to hold either.
lines.shot: drops both; slip "paraphrase · Portuguese governor (de Souza)"

lines.text: Chapter eight. Last to Leave.
And yet, Goa, Duh-mun and Dee-oo stayed Portuguese.
They outlasted the Mughals, the Marathas, even the British.
lines.shot: other powers' flags fade around them

lines.text: Only in nineteen sixty-one did India take them back,
lines.caps: only in *1961 | did India | take them *back,
lines.shot: era bar races to 1961, Indian tricolour rises over Goa

lines.text: four hundred and sixty-three years after da Gama reached Kalikut.
The first Europeans to arrive
lines.shot: the cold-open dawn sea, three caravels

lines.text: were the last to leave.
And it all began with three small ships,
and a taste for pepper.
lines.shot: peppercorn rolls into the sack (loops to cut 5), end card
